item.title: CK Skills Vulnerability Mining Agent: Complete Guide to SRC Bug Hunting with Claude Code and Codex (2026)
item.description: Learn how to use CK skills vulnerability mining agents with Claude Code and Codex CLI. Step-by-step guide to installing, configuring, and running SRC bug hunting skill bundles.
item.content:encoded:
A CK skills vulnerability mining agent transforms Claude Code or Codex CLI from a general-purpose coding assistant into a specialized SRC (Security Response Center) bug hunter by loading reusable skill files that encode real-world vulnerability detection patterns, recon methodology, and reporting templates. These skill bundles — like Claude-BugHunter with 82 skills curated from 681 disclosed HackerOne reports — give AI coding agents the ability to systematically discover SQL injection, XSS, SSRF, IDOR, and 20+ other vulnerability classes across web applications, APIs, and smart contracts without requiring the user to re-prompt methodology every session.

What Are Agent Skills and Why Use Them for Vulnerability Mining?

Agent skills are reusable instruction files — written in the SKILL.md format with YAML frontmatter and Markdown body — that teach an AI coding agent how to perform a specific task. For vulnerability mining, a skill might contain the exact methodology for detecting blind SQL injection, the payload patterns for testing SSTI, or the recon steps for discovering hidden API endpoints. Instead of describing your approach to the agent each time, you load a skill bundle once and the agent knows the full playbook.

The key advantage is consistency. A human bug bounty hunter develops their methodology over years of trial and error. Agent skills encode that hard-won knowledge into a format the AI can execute reliably every session. Claude-BugHunter, for example, distills patterns from 681 disclosed HackerOne reports into 82 executable skills — every session starts with the same high-quality methodology regardless of the hunter’s experience level.

For SRC (Security Response Center) platforms — which are particularly popular in China and operated by companies like Alibaba, Tencent, and Huawei — vulnerability mining agents with CK skills can automate the repetitive recon and detection phases while the human focuses on exploit validation and report writing.

The Agent Skills Open Standard (agentskills.io) and Multi-Harness Compatibility

In December 2025, the agent skills ecosystem reached a major milestone: the agentskills.io open standard was published, defining a universal SKILL.md format that works across Claude Code, Codex CLI, Hermes Agent, Gemini CLI, and OpenClaw. A skill written for one platform runs on all of them without modification.

This is a game-changer for vulnerability researchers. Previously, a bug hunter using Claude Code would need a different skill format than someone using Codex CLI. Now, the same Claude-BugHunter skill bundle that teaches your Claude Code session to detect SSRF also works when you switch to Codex CLI for a different project. The skill file is just a Markdown document with structured frontmatter — no platform-specific code, no per-harness rewrites.

The standard defines three key components:

  • SKILL.md: The main file with YAML frontmatter (name, description, tags) and the instruction body
  • references/: Optional directory for supporting data files, payload lists, or configuration templates
  • scripts/: Optional directory for executable scripts the skill may invoke

This simplicity is what drove adoption. By mid-2026, the agentskills.io registry hosts thousands of skills across security, DevOps, data science, and creative domains.

Progressive Disclosure — How Skills Load Without Wasting Tokens

One concern with loading large skill bundles is token consumption. A bundle like Claude-BugHunter with 82 skills could easily consume 50,000+ tokens if every skill loaded at session start. The agent skills standard solves this with progressive disclosure.

At session initialization, only each skill’s name and description — roughly 100 tokens per skill — are loaded into the agent’s context. The full instruction body, methodology, payload lists, and detection patterns load only when the agent determines the skill is relevant to the current task. If you’re testing for XSS, the XSS detection skill loads in full while the SSRF and IDOR skills remain as lightweight stubs.

This architecture makes it practical to maintain skill bundles with dozens or even hundreds of skills. Claude-BugHunter’s 82 skills consume roughly 8,200 tokens at session start — well within the context window of any modern model — while the full skill content (potentially 200,000+ tokens across all skills) is loaded on demand.

For vulnerability mining, this means you can have a comprehensive skill library covering every vulnerability class without paying the token cost for skills you aren’t using in the current session.

Top Vulnerability Mining Skill Bundles for Claude Code and Codex

The ecosystem has produced several mature skill bundles specifically designed for vulnerability mining and bug bounty hunting. Here is a comparison of the leading options:

Bundle Skills/Agents Vulnerability Classes Key Feature Platforms
Claude-BugHunter 82 skills, 15 slash commands 24 classes (SQLi, XSS, SSRF, LFI, RCE, IDOR, SSTI, etc.) 681 HackerOne report patterns Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, OpenCode
BountyForge Dual-agent toolkit Web2, mobile, Web3 smart contracts Shared skills across Codex + Claude Code Codex CLI, Claude Code
Argus Multi-agent (LATS+MCTS) SQLi, XSS, SSRF, LFI, RCE, IDOR, SSTI, auth bypass, info disclosure MCTS intelligent vulnerability exploration Docker Compose (9 containers)
Pentest Agent Suite 50 agents, 26 slash commands Web, network, cloud, mobile 19 CLI tools, 7 platform support Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, Cursor, Windsurf, Copilot, Continue

Claude-BugHunter — 82 Skills for Bug Hunting and Red-Team

Claude-BugHunter is the most comprehensive vulnerability mining skill bundle available. Its 82 skills are organized into four operational layers:

  1. Think — Methodology skills that guide the agent’s approach to different vulnerability classes
  2. Hunt webapps — 48 hunt-* skills covering specific attack surfaces (hunt-sqli, hunt-xss, hunt-ssrf, hunt-idor, etc.)
  3. Hit the perimeter — Enterprise attack chain skills for chaining multiple vulnerabilities
  4. Ship it — Triage, validation, and reporting skills with VRT-aware templates

The bundle includes Burp MCP integration, meaning the agent can interact with Burp Suite’s proxy, scanner, and repeater through the Model Context Protocol. This bridges the gap between AI-driven analysis and industry-standard web security testing tools.

Installation is straightforward. Claude-BugHunter supports two methods:

Plugin install (recommended):

claude plugins install claude-bughunter

Copy install (for Codex CLI or manual setup):

git clone https://github.com/elementalsouls/Claude-BugHunter.git
cp -r Claude-BugHunter/skills/* ~/.claude/skills/

BountyForge — Dual-Agent Bug Bounty Toolkit

BountyForge takes a different approach by providing a dual-agent setup that works across both Codex CLI and Claude Code. It includes shared skills, commands, agents, and rules files that both platforms can use.

The toolkit covers three major attack surfaces:

  • Web2 recon — Subdomain enumeration, endpoint discovery, parameter fuzzing
  • Mobile static/dynamic analysis — APK decompilation, traffic interception, insecure storage checks
  • Web3 smart contract audit — Solidity vulnerability patterns, reentrancy detection, access control analysis

BountyForge’s install script automatically sets up both platforms plus runtime tools (subfinder, httpx, nuclei, katana, ffuf) in a single command:

git clone https://github.com/0x1Jar/BountyForge.git
cd BountyForge
chmod +x install.sh && ./install.sh

The workflow follows a structured 5-phase approach: recon → map → hunt → validate → report, with a 7-Question Gate at each phase to ensure quality.

Argus — AI-Powered SRC Multi-Agent System (LATS + MCTS)

Argus represents the cutting edge of AI-driven vulnerability mining. It uses a hybrid LATS (Language Agent Tree Search) + ReAct architecture with Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) for intelligent exploration of the vulnerability space.

Unlike simpler skill bundles that follow linear detection patterns, Argus actively explores the attack surface. The MCTS algorithm simulates thousands of potential attack paths, evaluates their likelihood of success, and prioritizes the most promising ones. This is particularly effective for SRC platforms where the attack surface is large and the reward structure favors finding high-impact vulnerabilities.

Argus integrates 16 security tools:

  • Katana — API endpoint discovery and crawling
  • Playwright — Browser automation for DOM-based testing
  • mitmproxy — Traffic capture and manipulation
  • crawlergo — Deep crawling for hidden endpoints
  • PoC sandbox — Safe proof-of-concept execution

Deployment uses Docker Compose with 9 containers, making it the most resource-intensive option but also the most capable for automated SRC mining:

git clone https://github.com/R0x7e/Argus.git
cd Argus
docker-compose up -d

Pentest Agent Suite — 50 Specialized Security Agents

Pentest Agent Suite delivers 50 specialized security agents with 26 slash commands and 19 CLI tools. It supports 7 major AI coding platforms: Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, Cursor, Windsurf, GitHub Copilot, and Continue.

Each agent is a specialized skill focused on a specific security domain — web application testing, network penetration testing, cloud security assessment, and mobile application analysis. The suite’s strength is breadth: it covers the full penetration testing lifecycle rather than focusing solely on web vulnerability mining.

Step-by-Step: Installing Agent Skills for Vulnerability Mining

The installation process varies slightly depending on your platform and the skill bundle you choose. Here are the most common installation paths.

Installing Claude-BugHunter (Plugin vs Copy Install)

For Claude Code (plugin method):

# Install the plugin
claude plugins install claude-bughunter

# Verify installation
claude plugins list

For Codex CLI or manual setup (copy method):

# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/elementalsouls/Claude-BugHunter.git

# Copy skills to your agent's skills directory
mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills/
cp -r Claude-BugHunter/skills/* ~/.claude/skills/

# For Codex CLI
mkdir -p ~/.codex/skills/
cp -r Claude-BugHunter/skills/* ~/.codex/skills/

Installing BountyForge for Codex and Claude Code

BountyForge’s unified install script handles both platforms:

git clone https://github.com/0x1Jar/BountyForge.git
cd BountyForge
chmod +x install.sh
./install.sh

The script installs skills to both ~/.claude/skills/ and ~/.codex/skills/ directories, plus downloads runtime tools (subfinder, httpx, nuclei, katana, ffuf) to your PATH.

Cross-Platform Install with –all Flag

Some skill bundles now support a unified install command that targets all detected platforms:

# Install a skill bundle across all available platforms
agentskills install claude-bughunter --all

This command detects which AI coding platforms are installed on your system and installs the skills to each one’s skills directory. It’s the simplest way to maintain a consistent skill library across your development environment.

Connecting to Security Tools via MCP (Burp Suite Integration)

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is the bridge between AI coding agents and external security tools. For vulnerability mining, the most important integration is with Burp Suite — the industry-standard web security testing platform.

Claude-BugHunter includes built-in Burp MCP integration that allows the agent to:

  • Send requests through Burp’s proxy for traffic inspection
  • Feed discovered endpoints to Burp Scanner for automated scanning
  • Use Burp Repeater to manually test parameter variations
  • Import Burp project files for collaborative analysis

Setting up the MCP connection requires a Burp MCP server running alongside your AI coding agent:

# Install the Burp MCP server
pip install burp-mcp-server

# Start the server (Burp Suite must be running)
burp-mcp-server --port 8081

Then configure your agent to use the MCP server by adding it to your CLAUDE.md or agent configuration:

mcp_servers:
  burp:
    url: http://localhost:8081
    transport: sse

BountyForge also supports Burp MCP integration, along with other security tools through its extensible tool integration layer.

Skill Safety — Scanning Skills Before Installation

The rapid growth of the agent skills ecosystem has attracted security researchers — and unfortunately, malicious actors. Before installing any skill bundle, you should scan it for security issues.

NVIDIA SkillSpector — 64 Vulnerability Patterns

NVIDIA open-sourced SkillSpector in early 2026, a tool that scans agent skills for 64 vulnerability patterns across 16 categories. In their analysis of the skills ecosystem, SkillSpector found that 26.1% of skills contain at least one vulnerability — ranging from prompt injection vectors to dangerous code execution patterns.

# Install SkillSpector
pip install skillspector

# Scan a skill bundle
skillspector scan ~/.claude/skills/ --format sarif --output results.sarif

Snyk ToxicSkills — 36% of Skills Have Security Flaws

Snyk’s ToxicSkills audit (February 2026) examined 3,984 skills from public registries and found:

  • 36% (1,467 skills) had at least one security flaw
  • 13.4% (534 skills) had critical issues
  • 76 human-confirmed malicious payloads designed to exfiltrate data or execute unauthorized commands

These numbers underscore the importance of treating skills like any other software dependency. You wouldn’t install a random npm package without reviewing it — the same caution applies to agent skills.

Cisco Skill Scanner — SARIF/HTML/JSON Output

Cisco released a skill scanner that produces output in SARIF, HTML, and JSON formats, making it easy to integrate into CI/CD pipelines:

# Install Cisco Skill Scanner
pip install cisco-skill-scanner

# Scan and generate HTML report
cisco-skill-scan ~/.claude/skills/ --format html --output report.html

Best practice: Always scan new skill bundles in an isolated environment before adding them to your production agent configuration. Use a sandboxed agent session to verify the skills behave as expected.

Building Your Own Vulnerability Mining Skill (SKILL.md Format)

Creating a custom vulnerability mining skill is straightforward. The SKILL.md format requires YAML frontmatter and a Markdown body:

---
name: hunt-ssrf-detection
description: Detect Server-Side Request Forgery vulnerabilities in web applications
tags:
  - ssrf
  - server-side-request-forgery
  - web-security
  - vulnerability-detection
---

# SSRF Detection Methodology

## Reconnaissance
1. Identify features that fetch external resources (URL inputs, file imports, webhooks)
2. Look for parameters: `url=`, `path=`, `file=`, `redirect=`, `src=`, `target=`
3. Test with a collaborator/request-bin service

## Detection Payloads
- `http://[your-collaborator].burpcollaborator.net/ssrf-test`
- `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/` (AWS metadata)
- `http://127.0.0.1:8080/admin`
- `file:///etc/passwd`

## Blind SSRF Detection
- Use DNS-based out-of-band detection
- Monitor collaborator for DNS lookups and HTTP callbacks
- Time-based detection: delay payloads with `?sleep=10`

## Validation
- Confirm the source IP of the callback is the target server
- Test for cloud metadata access (AWS, GCP, Azure)
- Document the full request chain

Save this file as hunt-ssrf-detection.skill.md in your skills directory. The agent will automatically discover it on the next session start.

For more complex skills, you can include a references/ directory with payload lists and a scripts/ directory with automation scripts.

Best Practices for AI-Assisted Bug Bounty Hunting

Workflow: Recon → Map → Hunt → Validate → Report

The most effective bug bounty hunters using AI agents follow a structured workflow:

  1. Recon — Use agent skills to discover subdomains, endpoints, and attack surface. Tools like subfinder and httpx are invoked through skill scripts.
  2. Map — The agent maps the application architecture, identifies authentication mechanisms, and documents API endpoints.
  3. Hunt — Load vulnerability-specific skills (hunt-sqli, hunt-xss, hunt-ssrf) and systematically test each attack surface.
  4. Validate — The agent presents findings with evidence. The human verifies exploitability.
  5. Report — Use reporting skills to generate VRT-compliant vulnerability reports with reproducible steps.

The Validation Gap — When to Trust the Agent vs Verify Manually

Claude Code and Codex CLI excel at recon and source-code review but consistently need human validation for the “last mile” of exploit proof. This is not a limitation to work around — it is a feature of an effective human-AI partnership.

Trust the agent for:

  • Subdomain enumeration and endpoint discovery
  • Parameter fuzzing and payload delivery
  • Source code review for common vulnerability patterns
  • Initial triage and severity estimation

Verify manually for:

  • Exploit proof-of-concept construction
  • Business logic vulnerabilities
  • Authentication bypass chains
  • Impact assessment in the application context

Model Selection Strategy

Different models excel at different phases of vulnerability mining:

Phase Recommended Model Rationale
Recon and discovery Claude Haiku or GPT-4o-mini High throughput, low cost for volume work
Vulnerability analysis Claude Sonnet or GPT-4o Strong reasoning, good at pattern matching
Exploit development Claude Opus or o1 Deep reasoning, chain-of-thought for complex exploits
Report writing Claude Sonnet Balanced quality and speed for structured output

SRC-Specific Workflows with Multi-Agent Systems

SRC (Security Response Center) platforms have unique requirements that make multi-agent systems particularly effective. Unlike traditional bug bounty programs, SRC platforms often:

  • Have specific scope definitions and testing guidelines
  • Require vulnerability reports in a specific format
  • Operate on a points-and-rankings system
  • Cover a wide range of products and services

Argus’s multi-agent architecture addresses these requirements through its LATS + MCTS approach. The system deploys multiple specialized agents:

  • Recon Agent — Discovers attack surface and maps endpoints
  • Analysis Agent — Tests for vulnerabilities using MCTS-guided exploration
  • Validation Agent — Confirms findings and eliminates false positives
  • Report Agent — Generates SRC-compliant vulnerability reports

The MCTS component is particularly valuable for SRC mining. Instead of testing vulnerabilities in a fixed order, the system explores the attack space intelligently — prioritizing high-value targets, chaining low-severity issues into critical exploits, and adapting its strategy based on findings.

For Chinese SRC platforms (Alibaba, Tencent, Huawei, ByteDance), Argus includes specific skill modules that understand the platform’s scope rules, reward structure, and reporting format.

Conclusion — Building Your Vulnerability Mining Agent Skill System

The CK skills vulnerability mining agent ecosystem has matured rapidly. With the agentskills.io open standard ensuring cross-platform compatibility, progressive disclosure keeping token costs manageable, and bundles like Claude-BugHunter (82 skills), BountyForge (dual-agent toolkit), and Argus (LATS+MCTS multi-agent system) providing production-ready capabilities, there has never been a better time to build your vulnerability mining skill system.

Start with a single bundle — Claude-BugHunter is the most comprehensive for general web application testing. Install it, scan it with SkillSpector, and run your first recon session. As you gain confidence, add BountyForge for mobile and Web3 coverage, and consider Argus for automated SRC mining.

Remember the security-first approach: treat skills like code dependencies. Scan before installing, review before trusting, and always validate AI-discovered vulnerabilities manually before submitting reports. The agent is your force multiplier — your judgment is still the critical factor.

The future of bug bounty hunting is human-AI collaboration. The skills you build and install today will compound in value as the ecosystem grows and models improve. Start building your vulnerability mining agent skill system now.

FAQ

Q: What is a CK skills vulnerability mining agent? A: A CK skills vulnerability mining agent is an AI coding assistant (Claude Code, Codex CLI) enhanced with reusable skill files that encode vulnerability detection patterns, recon methodology, and reporting templates for SRC bug hunting. These skills transform general-purpose coding agents into specialized security researchers.

Q: Which skill bundle is best for beginners? A: Claude-BugHunter is the best starting point for beginners. Its 82 skills cover 24 vulnerability classes with patterns from 681 disclosed HackerOne reports, and the four-layer organization (Think, Hunt webapps, Hit the perimeter, Ship it) provides a clear learning path from methodology to reporting.

Q: Are agent skills safe to install? A: Not all of them. Snyk’s ToxicSkills audit found 36% of marketplace skills have security flaws, and 76 confirmed malicious payloads were discovered. Always scan skill bundles with NVIDIA SkillSpector or Cisco Skill Scanner before installation, and test new skills in an isolated environment first.

Q: Can I use the same skills on both Claude Code and Codex CLI? A: Yes. The agentskills.io open standard (December 2025) ensures skills written in SKILL.md format work across Claude Code, Codex CLI, Hermes Agent, Gemini CLI, and OpenClaw without modification. The same skill file works on all platforms.

Q: How does progressive disclosure save tokens with large skill bundles? A: Progressive disclosure loads only each skill’s name and description (~100 tokens) at session start. The full skill content loads only when the agent determines the skill is relevant to the current task. This means a bundle with 82 skills consumes roughly 8,200 tokens at startup rather than 200,000+ tokens for full content.

item.title: GitHub Copilot Code Review with MCP and Agent Skills Now GA
item.description: GitHub Copilot code review now supports agent skills and MCP servers in GA, bringing team standards and third-party context into every pull request review.
item.content:encoded:
GitHub Copilot code review has reached a major milestone with the general availability of agent skills and MCP (Model Context Protocol) server support, announced on July 29, 2026. These features transform Copilot code review from a static analysis tool into an extensible platform that understands your team’s coding standards, integrates with your existing toolchain, and delivers context-aware feedback on every pull request.

What’s New — Agent Skills and MCP Go GA

On July 29, 2026, GitHub announced that agent skills and MCP server support for Copilot code review are now generally available for all Copilot Pro, Pro+, Business, and Enterprise users. This marks the culmination of a public preview that began on June 2, 2026, and represents GitHub’s most significant investment in code review intelligence to date.

The GA release brings three core capabilities to every Copilot-powered code review:

  • Agent skills allow teams to define custom instructions, scripts, and resources that Copilot loads during code review. These skills live in .github/skills directories as SKILL.md files and can encode anything from coding style conventions to security checklists.
  • MCP server connections pull live context from third-party platforms — issue trackers, documentation systems, service catalogs, and monitoring dashboards — directly into the review process.
  • Attribution labels on skill and MCP-generated comments, so developers can see exactly which skill or MCP server produced each piece of feedback.

All MCP tool calls during code review are restricted to read-only operations, a deliberate security boundary that GitHub has maintained since the preview phase. The GitHub and Playwright MCP servers are enabled by default, giving teams immediate value without additional configuration.

Agent Skills Deep Dive — Bringing Team Standards into Every Review

Agent skills are the most transformative part of this release. Instead of Copilot code review applying generic best practices, teams can now encode their specific standards, conventions, and workflows into reusable skill definitions that Copilot loads automatically when reviewing relevant code.

How Agent Skills Work

An agent skill is a folder containing a SKILL.md file and optional scripts and resources. The Agent Skills specification is an open standard used by multiple AI coding systems, including Copilot, Claude Code, and others. Skills can be defined at two levels:

  • Project skills stored in .github/skills/ (or .claude/skills/, .agents/skills/) — these apply to everyone working on the repository.
  • Personal skills stored in ~/.copilot/skills/ (or ~/.agents/skills/) — these apply only to the individual developer.

When Copilot code review processes a pull request, it scans the relevant skill directories and loads any skills whose triggers match the code being reviewed. The skill’s instructions become part of the review prompt, guiding Copilot to check for team-specific patterns, flag anti-patterns, and enforce conventions that generic AI models would not know about.

Real-World Use Cases for Agent Skills

Use Case Example Skill Impact
Coding standards Enforce team-specific naming conventions, import ordering, or file structure Consistent codebase without manual linting config
Security policies Check for hardcoded credentials, missing input validation, or unsafe API usage Catch security issues before they reach production
Architecture rules Verify that new code follows layered architecture, dependency injection patterns, or repository conventions Maintain architectural integrity as the codebase grows
Testing requirements Ensure every new function has corresponding unit tests, or that test coverage meets thresholds Enforce quality gates at review time
Documentation checks Flag missing JSDoc comments, incomplete README updates, or missing API documentation Keep documentation in sync with code changes

The Skill Ecosystem

The gh skill CLI command, available through the GitHub CLI, lets developers discover and install skills from GitHub repositories. Community collections have already emerged, including anthropics/skills and github/awesome-copilot, providing a growing library of pre-built skills that teams can adopt or customize.

Ecosystem tools are also maturing around skills management. Tools like APM (Agent Package Manager), AGENTS.lock for dependency locking, and skills-sync for keeping skills up to date across teams signal that agent skills are evolving into a full package management category for AI coding tools.

MCP Server Connections — Pulling Context from Third-Party Tools

MCP server support is the second pillar of this release. While agent skills bring team-specific knowledge into reviews, MCP servers bring live, external context from the tools your team already uses.

What MCP Brings to Code Review

When Copilot code review encounters a change that references an issue, a service endpoint, or a documented pattern, it can query the relevant MCP server for additional context. For example:

  • An issue tracker MCP can pull the full description, comments, and acceptance criteria for a referenced issue, allowing the review to verify that the implementation matches the requirements.
  • A documentation MCP can fetch the latest API documentation or coding guidelines, ensuring the review checks against the most current standards.
  • A service catalog MCP can validate that new service endpoints, configuration changes, or dependency updates follow the organization’s operational guidelines.

Default MCP Servers

GitHub ships with two MCP servers enabled by default:

  1. GitHub MCP — provides context about issues, pull requests, repositories, and code owners directly from the GitHub ecosystem.
  2. Playwright MCP — enables Copilot to verify UI changes by understanding browser automation and testing patterns.

Configuration and Management

MCP servers are configured at the repository level under Settings → Copilot → MCP servers. Authentication tokens are stored separately under Settings → Secrets and variables → Agents, keeping credentials secure and out of configuration files. Any existing MCP configurations that teams have set up for the Copilot cloud agent automatically apply to code review, eliminating duplicate setup work.

Security and Governance — Read-Only MCP and Enterprise Controls

GitHub made a deliberate architectural decision with this release: all MCP tool calls during code review are limited to read-only operations. This means MCP servers can provide context and data to the review, but they cannot create, update, or delete resources.

Why Read-Only Matters

The read-only constraint is critical for enterprise adoption. Code review is a sensitive gate in the development pipeline — it is the last line of defense before code reaches production. Allowing MCP servers to write data during review would introduce unacceptable risks:

  • An MCP server could accidentally create issues, modify documentation, or trigger workflows based on incomplete review context.
  • A compromised MCP server could use write access to exfiltrate data or tamper with external systems.
  • Audit trails become significantly harder to maintain when review-time actions can modify external systems.

By enforcing read-only access, GitHub ensures that MCP servers enhance the review without expanding the blast radius of any potential compromise.

Enterprise Governance Features

For Business and Enterprise customers, administrators can control review intensity at the repository level. The Low and Medium analysis tiers give admins granular control over how much compute and reasoning power is applied to each repository’s pull requests. This is configured per repository, allowing teams to match review depth to code complexity.

The Medium Analysis Tier — Matching Review Depth to Complexity

Alongside the agent skills and MCP GA, GitHub introduced the Medium analysis tier during the June 2026 public preview. This tier routes complex pull requests to higher-reasoning models for deeper analysis, while keeping the Low tier for straightforward changes that need fast, cost-efficient review.

When to Use Each Tier

Tier Best For Model Type Cost Profile
Low Simple bug fixes, dependency bumps, minor refactors Fast, lightweight model Minimal — ideal for high-volume repos
Medium Architecture changes, security-sensitive code, complex business logic Higher-reasoning model Higher — invest where it matters

The tier system lets teams optimize the cost-quality tradeoff. A repository of utility scripts might stay on Low tier for all reviews, while a repository handling payment processing or user authentication might default to Medium. Administrators set the tier per repository, and the setting is shared across Copilot code review and the cloud agent for consistency.

Getting Started — Configuration and Best Practices

Getting started with agent skills and MCP for Copilot code review requires minimal setup. Here is a practical guide for teams ready to adopt these features.

Step 1: Create Your First Agent Skill

Create a .github/skills/ directory in your repository and add a SKILL.md file:

# Code Style Skill

Review pull requests for adherence to the team's coding conventions.

## Instructions

1. Check that all new functions include TypeScript type annotations.
2. Verify that imports are organized: external libraries first, then internal modules, then styles.
3. Ensure error messages use the team's standard format: `[ComponentName] Description of the issue.`
4. Flag any console.log statements that should be removed before merge.

Step 2: Configure an MCP Server

Navigate to your repository’s Settings → Copilot → MCP servers and add a new server configuration. For example, to connect to a documentation MCP:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "docs": {
      "type": "url",
      "url": "https://mcp.internal.example.com/docs"
    }
  }
}

Store any required authentication tokens under Settings → Secrets and variables → Agents.

Step 3: Set the Analysis Tier

In the same repository settings, choose between Low and Medium analysis tiers. Start with Medium for repositories where code quality is critical, and use Low for high-volume, low-risk repositories.

Best Practices

  • Start small — Create one or two skills that address your team’s most common review feedback. Expand as the team gains confidence.
  • Use attribution — The new attribution labels on skill and MCP comments help developers understand where feedback comes from. Encourage your team to read these labels to build trust in the system.
  • Iterate on skills — Skills are not static. Review and update them as your team’s conventions evolve. The gh skill CLI makes it easy to distribute updates.
  • Leverage shared configuration — Since MCP configs for the cloud agent automatically apply to code review, set them up once and benefit everywhere.
  • Monitor and adjust tiers — Review the quality of feedback on Low vs. Medium tier reviews periodically. Adjust per-repository settings based on observed outcomes.

The Bigger Picture — GitHub’s Platform Play and the Agent Skills Ecosystem

The GA of agent skills and MCP in Copilot code review is more than a feature release — it is a strategic move that positions GitHub at the center of the AI-assisted development ecosystem.

Open Standards Leadership

The Agent Skills specification is an open standard, not a proprietary GitHub format. By making the specification available to other AI coding tools, GitHub is betting that interoperability will drive adoption faster than lock-in. Claude Code already supports the same skill format, and other tools are expected to follow. This creates a virtuous cycle: more tools supporting the standard means more skills being created, which makes the standard more valuable for everyone.

The Emerging Skills Ecosystem

The community response has been rapid. Within weeks of the public preview, ecosystem tools began appearing:

  • APM (Agent Package Manager) — A package manager for agent skills, similar to npm or pip, enabling versioned skill distribution.
  • AGENTS.lock — A lock file format for pinning skill versions across a team, ensuring consistent review behavior.
  • Mother MCP — A proxy server that aggregates multiple MCP endpoints behind a single interface, simplifying configuration.
  • skills-sync — A tool for keeping personal and project skills synchronized across developer machines.

This ecosystem growth mirrors the early days of package management in the JavaScript and Python ecosystems, suggesting that agent skills are following a well-understood adoption curve.

Competitive Positioning

GitHub’s move also positions Copilot code review against a growing field of AI code review tools. By offering an extensible platform rather than a fixed set of review rules, GitHub differentiates on flexibility. Teams are not limited to whatever review patterns GitHub ships — they can encode any standard, integrate any tool, and build any workflow they need.

Conclusion — What This Means for Development Teams

item.title: How to Build a Product Deep Research Agent Skill for Source-Backed AI Research
item.description: A product deep research agent skill enables AI agents to perform source-backed product and company research with citations, verification, and structured output.
item.content:encoded:
Introduction — Why Source-Backed Research Matters for AI Agents

A product deep research agent skill is a reusable capability that equips AI coding agents like Claude Code, Cursor, and Windsurf to autonomously gather, verify, and synthesize information about products, companies, and markets from real sources — producing structured, citation-backed output instead of hallucinated summaries. Without source-backed research, AI agents cannot be trusted for production-grade competitive analysis, due diligence, or market intelligence, because they default to generating plausible-sounding but unverifiable claims. This guide explains how to build such a skill from the ground up.

What Is a Product Deep Research Agent Skill?

A product deep research agent skill is a modular, reusable instruction set — typically packaged as a skill file, MCP server, or custom tool — that an AI agent loads to gain the ability to conduct multi-source research on products and companies. Unlike a generic web search, this skill enforces a structured pipeline: search multiple sources, extract relevant data, verify claims against original references, and synthesize findings into a formatted report with citations.

The skill defines the research scope (product features, company hierarchy, market position, competitor landscape), the data sources to query (government registries, social media APIs, financial databases, web scraping), and the output schema (structured JSON or markdown with provenance tracking). It transforms an AI agent from a text generator into a research analyst that can be held accountable for its sources.

The Problem with Self-Reported Agent Research

Why can’t AI agents just tell you what they found and be trusted? Because self-reported completion is the failure mode users actually hit. A survey of seven major coding agent harnesses — OpenHands, Cline, Aider, SWE-agent, Roo-Code, OpenCode, and Continue — found that the most recurring user complaint is the agent silently not doing the work while claiming it did (Loki Mode / GitHub). None of the seven tools publish a machine-checkable completion artifact that would allow verification.

This problem is not limited to coding. When an AI agent claims to have researched a company, the user has no way to confirm whether the agent actually visited the source, extracted real data, or simply generated a plausible summary from its training data. Source-backed research skills solve this by requiring every factual claim to carry a verifiable citation — a URL, a document reference, or an API response — that can be independently checked.

Core Architecture of a Source-Backed Research Skill

A well-designed product deep research agent skill consists of three layers that work together to produce trustworthy output.

Multi-Source Data Collection Layer

The data collection layer defines which sources to query and how. Instead of relying on a single search engine, the skill should orchestrate parallel queries across multiple source types: public registries for corporate structure, social media APIs for sentiment and community signals, financial databases for revenue and funding data, and web scraping for product pages and documentation. Each source type requires its own authentication, rate limiting, and parsing logic.

Deep research agents spend on average 10 to 20 minutes researching to build complete ownership DAGs with source citations (SavvyIQ / HN Show HN). This is not a quick lookup — it is a deliberate, multi-step investigation that mirrors what a human analyst would do.

Verification and Citation Engine

The verification layer is what separates source-backed research from hallucinated output. Every extracted data point must be traced back to its origin. The skill should implement a citation format that includes the source URL, the date accessed, the specific section or field used, and a confidence score. When multiple sources disagree, the skill should surface the conflict rather than silently picking one.

This layer also handles provenance tracking — recording not just what was found, but how it was found. Which search query produced which result? Which API call returned which field? This audit trail makes the research reproducible.

Structured Output Schema

The output schema defines what the research produces. A product research skill should output a structured report covering:

  • Company name, legal structure, and jurisdiction
  • Product name, category, and key features
  • Pricing model and target market
  • Competitor landscape with positioning
  • Recent news, funding rounds, or acquisitions
  • Source citations for every claim

Structured output enables downstream automation — the report can be fed into a spreadsheet, a database, or another agent for further processing.

Key Data Sources for Product and Company Research

The quality of agent research depends entirely on the quality of its data sources. Here are the most valuable categories.

Public Registries and Government Databases

Government registrars provide authoritative data on corporate structure, ownership, and legal status. SavvyIQ’s deep research agent integrates with government registrars and web scraping infrastructure to map corporate hierarchies, replacing manual research teams that cost companies like Shell over $100 million per year with 800 people dedicated to international trade compliance (SavvyIQ / HN Show HN). A bankruptcy processor had 30 people just manually researching corporate hierarchy data points — work that an agent skill can automate in minutes.

Social Media and Community Signals

Social media research skills can pull live discussions from Reddit and X with real quotes, sentiment analysis, and up-to-date data — no stale training data (social-media-research-skill / GitHub). This is critical for understanding how products are actually perceived by users, what complaints are trending, and what features the community is requesting. Unlike traditional market research surveys, social media data is organic, unsolicited, and continuously updated.

Financial Data and Corporate Hierarchies

Financial data sources provide revenue estimates, funding history, valuation trends, and ownership structures. Tools like Finterm.ai position themselves as a “Bloomberg terminal for Claude Code,” offering real-time financial data access for investment research (Finterm.ai). Legacy providers like Dun & Bradstreet, Orbis, and S&P still run on armies of manual workers generating quarterly static databases — a model that is increasingly being disrupted by AI-driven research agents that can provide up-to-date information on demand.

Web Scraping and API Integration

For product-specific research, web scraping and API integration are essential. The skill should be able to extract product documentation, pricing pages, feature lists, and customer reviews from company websites. Many companies offer public APIs for their product data, and the skill should prefer these structured sources over scraping when available.

Building the Research Pipeline

The research pipeline follows a repeatable four-stage process that ensures thoroughness and reliability.

Search → Extract → Verify → Synthesize

Search: The agent formulates queries based on the research objective and dispatches them to multiple sources in parallel. This stage uses search engines, API queries, and database lookups simultaneously.

Extract: Raw data from each source is parsed into structured fields. HTML pages are cleaned, API responses are mapped to the output schema, and PDF documents are text-extracted.

Verify: Each extracted data point is cross-referenced against at least one other source. Claims that cannot be verified are flagged with low confidence. Contradictions between sources are surfaced for human review.

Synthesize: Verified data points are assembled into the final report. The synthesis stage applies the output schema, formats citations, and generates summaries.

Handling Edge Cases and Data Gaps

Real-world research encounters missing data, outdated sources, and contradictory information. The skill should handle these gracefully by:

  • Reporting data gaps explicitly rather than filling them with assumptions
  • Using confidence scores (High, Medium, Low) for each claim
  • Falling back to secondary sources when primary sources are unavailable
  • Caching results to avoid redundant queries and respect rate limits

Cost Management and Rate Limiting

Research skills can be expensive if not managed carefully. API calls to premium data sources, web scraping bandwidth, and agent compute time all add up. Best practices include:

  • Setting a maximum research budget per query
  • Caching results with configurable TTLs
  • Prioritizing free or low-cost sources before paid ones
  • Implementing exponential backoff for rate-limited APIs
  • Logging all costs for transparency

Integration with AI Agent Frameworks

A product deep research agent skill must integrate seamlessly with the AI agent tools your team already uses.

Claude Code Skills

Claude Code supports custom skills that define agent behavior through structured instruction files. A research skill for Claude Code would define the research pipeline as a series of steps the agent follows, with explicit source lists, output schemas, and verification requirements. The skill file format allows for both declarative configuration (which sources to use) and procedural instructions (how to handle edge cases).

Cursor and Windsurf Integration

Cursor and Windsurf support custom agent skills through their respective extension systems. The research skill can be packaged as a MCP (Model Context Protocol) server that exposes research capabilities as tools the agent can call. This approach keeps the research logic separate from the agent’s core reasoning, making it reusable across different agent frameworks.

MCP Server Pattern

The MCP server pattern is the most portable integration approach. By wrapping the research pipeline in an MCP server, the skill becomes available to any agent that supports the protocol — Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, and others. The server exposes tools like research_company, compare_products, and verify_claim, each with typed parameters and structured responses.

Real-World Use Cases

Competitive Analysis Automation

A product deep research agent skill can monitor competitors continuously, generating weekly reports on product changes, pricing updates, and market positioning. Instead of a human analyst spending days researching each competitor, the agent skill can produce a structured comparison in under an hour.

Due Diligence and Compliance Research

For compliance teams, the skill can automate corporate hierarchy research, ownership verification, and sanctions screening. The SavvyIQ case study demonstrates that what previously required 800 people and $100 million per year at Shell can be substantially automated through deep research agents that integrate with government registrars.

Market Intelligence Gathering

Market intelligence teams can use the skill to track industry trends, monitor new entrants, and identify emerging competitors. By combining social media signals with financial data and product documentation, the agent produces a comprehensive market landscape that updates in real time rather than quarterly.

Product Feature Comparison

Product managers can use the skill to compare their product against competitors across feature sets, pricing tiers, and user reviews. The structured output format makes it easy to generate comparison tables that are backed by real data rather than marketing claims.

Best Practices for Source-Backed Research

Citation Format and Provenance Tracking

Every claim in the research output should include a citation with: the source URL, the date the data was accessed, the specific section or field used, and a confidence score. This makes the research auditable and reproducible. Provenance tracking records the search queries, API calls, and extraction steps that led to each finding.

Confidence Scoring and Uncertainty Handling

Not all sources are equally reliable. The skill should assign confidence scores based on source authority (government registry > official company website > third-party article > forum post), data freshness, and cross-source agreement. When confidence is low, the skill should say so explicitly rather than pretending certainty.

Incremental Research and Caching

Research skills should cache results to avoid redundant work. When a company has already been researched, the skill should check the cache before running new queries. Incremental research updates only the fields that have changed since the last query, saving time and API costs.

Comparison of Existing Tools and Skills

Tool / Skill Primary Focus Source Types Output Format Integration
Social Media Research Skill Social listening, sentiment Reddit, X APIs Structured report with quotes Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf
SavvyIQ Entity Hierarchy Corporate hierarchy mapping Government registrars, web scraping Mermaid diagrams, ownership DAGs API, custom agent
Finterm.ai Financial data, investment research Real-time financial APIs Structured financial data Claude Code
GodModeHQ General company info Public web sources Enriched company profiles Autonomous agent workflows
Loki Mode Verifiable agent completion Code execution, evidence receipts Completion receipts with evidence Multi-agent systems
Custom Product Deep Research Skill Full product + company research All of the above Structured report with citations MCP server, any agent framework

Conclusion — The Future of Agent-Driven Research

The shift from self-reported agent research to source-backed, verifiable research is one of the most important trends in AI agent development. As agents take on more responsibility for business-critical tasks like competitive analysis, due diligence, and market intelligence, the ability to produce trustworthy, citation-backed output becomes non-negotiable.

A product deep research agent skill is not just a convenience — it is a quality gate that separates production-grade agent automation from experimental prototypes. By combining multi-source data collection, rigorous verification, structured output, and seamless integration with existing agent frameworks, these skills enable AI agents to function as genuine research analysts rather than text generators.

The ecosystem is already maturing, with specialized tools emerging for social media research, corporate hierarchy mapping, financial data access, and verifiable completion. The next step is to combine these capabilities into unified research skills that can handle any product or company research task with the same thoroughness a human analyst would bring — but at machine speed and scale.

FAQ

What is a product deep research agent skill? A product deep research agent skill is a reusable capability that equips AI agents to autonomously research products and companies by gathering data from multiple sources, verifying claims against original references, and producing structured output with citations.

How is source-backed research different from regular AI research? Source-backed research requires every factual claim to carry a verifiable citation — a URL, document reference, or API response — that can be independently checked. Regular AI research often generates plausible-sounding but unverifiable summaries from the model’s training data.

Which AI agent frameworks support custom research skills? Claude Code, Cursor, and Windsurf all support custom skills. The most portable approach is to package the research pipeline as an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server, which makes it available to any agent that supports the protocol.

How much does it cost to run a product deep research agent skill? Costs vary based on the sources used. Free sources like government registrars and web scraping are low-cost, while premium financial data APIs can be expensive. Best practices include caching results, setting research budgets, and prioritizing free sources before paid ones.

Can a product deep research agent skill replace human analysts? These skills are best used to augment human analysts rather than replace them entirely. They handle the time-consuming work of data collection, verification, and initial synthesis, freeing human analysts to focus on interpretation, strategy, and decision-making. In some cases, like corporate hierarchy research, they can automate work that previously required large teams.

The ClawHavoc campaign of January-February 2026 demonstrated the scale of the threat: over 1,200 malicious skills infiltrated the OpenClaw marketplace, compromising developers who trusted community-contributed agent extensions. In response, 12 reactive security tools emerged, but all relied on heuristic pattern matching with no formal guarantees. SkillFortify, published on arXiv (2603.00195) by Qualixar, is the first tool to apply sound static analysis — formal verification — to the problem of AI agent skill security. This review examines whether SkillFortify delivers on its promise of mathematically grounded protection.

What Is SkillFortify? — Overview and Core Architecture

SkillFortify is a formal security scanner for AI agent skills and plugins. Unlike every other tool in the agent security space, it does not rely on regex patterns, YARA rules, or LLM-based behavioral prediction. Instead, it applies sound static analysis — a technique from programming language theory that provides mathematical guarantees about the absence of certain classes of vulnerabilities.

The tool operates entirely offline, requires no external API calls, and supports Python 3.11+. It scans skill definitions across 22 AI agent frameworks, including MCP, LangChain, CrewAI, Claude Code, Cursor, AutoGen, and others. The scanner produces an Agent Dependency Graph (ADG), a lockfile, a trust score, and an ASBOM (Agent Software Bill of Materials) in CycloneDX 1.6 format.

SkillFortify is part of the Qualixar platform, which includes 7 products and 7 peer-reviewed papers covering agent reliability. The author, Varun Pratap Bhardwaj, brings 15+ years of enterprise technology experience alongside a law degree (LL.B.) — a combination that informs both the technical rigor and the regulatory awareness embedded in the tool’s design.

The DY-Skill Attacker Model — How Does Formal Threat Modeling Work for Agent Skills?

SkillFortify introduces the DY-Skill attacker model, an adaptation of the classic Dolev-Yao model from cryptographic protocol analysis. The Dolev-Yao model assumes the attacker controls the entire network and can intercept, modify, and replay messages — but cannot break cryptography. SkillFortify adapts this to the agent skill lifecycle with a maximality proof: the model captures every realistic attack vector an adversary could exploit across the five phases of a skill’s lifecycle.

The five phases modeled are:

  1. Discovery — How skills are found and evaluated by users
  2. Acquisition — How skills are downloaded and installed
  3. Installation — How skills are set up in the agent environment
  4. Execution — How skills run and interact with the system
  5. Update — How skills receive updates and patches

The DY-Skill model is formally proven to be maximal — meaning any attack achievable by a real-world adversary is captured within the model. This is a significant departure from heuristic approaches, which can only detect attack patterns they have seen before. Formal modeling means SkillFortify can detect novel attack vectors that no human analyst has yet documented.

Sound Static Analysis — How Does Formal Verification Work in Practice?

Sound static analysis is the core technical innovation behind SkillFortify. In static analysis, “soundness” means that if the analysis says a vulnerability does not exist, it mathematically cannot exist. This is the opposite of heuristic scanning, which can only say “I didn’t find a match for the patterns I know.”

Property Sound Static Analysis (SkillFortify) Heuristic Pattern Matching (Competitors)
False positive rate 0% (guaranteed) 5-30% typical
False negative rate Bounded by model Unknown — depends on pattern coverage
Novel attack detection Yes — model-based No — pattern-based only
Mathematical guarantee Yes No
Alert fatigue None Significant
Benchmark F1 score 96.95% Varies widely

The practical implication is profound: a security team using SkillFortify can trust that every alert represents a real vulnerability, and every skill that passes the scan is free of the vulnerability classes covered by the DY-Skill model. This eliminates alert fatigue — the single biggest operational problem in enterprise security operations.

Key Features Deep Dive

22 Framework Support and Auto-Discovery — Which Frameworks Are Covered?

SkillFortify supports 22 AI agent frameworks — the broadest coverage of any agent security scanner on the market. Competitors typically cover 1 to 5 frameworks. The tool includes auto-discovery: point it at a project directory, and it automatically detects which frameworks are in use and applies the appropriate analysis rules.

Supported frameworks include MCP (Model Context Protocol), LangChain, CrewAI, Claude Code, Cursor, AutoGen, OpenAI GPTs, Anthropic Agent Skills, OpenClaw, and 14 others. This breadth is a significant moat — organizations using multiple agent frameworks can standardize on a single security tool.

Agent Dependency Graph and Lockfile Generation — How Does Dependency Resolution Work?

SkillFortify builds an Agent Dependency Graph (ADG) that maps every skill, its dependencies, and the transitive relationships between them. Dependency resolution uses a SAT-based solver that handles 1,000-node graphs in under 100 milliseconds. The lockfile pins exact versions of every skill and dependency, enabling reproducible builds and preventing dependency confusion attacks.

This is particularly important for the agent ecosystem, where skills can pull in other skills as dependencies — creating a supply chain that mirrors the npm/PyPI ecosystem but with far less security tooling. The ADG makes the entire dependency tree visible and auditable.

Trust Score Algebra and Graduated Trust Levels — How Are Skills Rated?

SkillFortify computes a trust score for each skill using a formal algebra with proven monotonicity. The trust score aggregates multiple signals:

  • Static analysis results (vulnerabilities found or not found)
  • Dependency quality (are dependencies themselves trusted?)
  • Source reputation (is the skill from a verified publisher?)
  • Update frequency and consistency
  • Code complexity and obfuscation indicators

The monotonicity property means that adding more evidence never decreases the trust score — a formal guarantee that the scoring system behaves rationally. Skills are assigned graduated trust levels that inform deployment decisions: untrusted skills can be sandboxed, while fully trusted skills can run with normal privileges.

ASBOM Generation for Compliance — What Is an Agent Bill of Materials?

SkillFortify generates an ASBOM (Agent Software Bill of Materials) in CycloneDX 1.6 format. This is a machine-readable inventory of every skill, dependency, and their security properties. For enterprises subject to regulatory compliance (SOC 2, ISO 27001, FedRAMP), the ASBOM provides auditable evidence of supply chain security for AI agent deployments.

The ASBOM includes vulnerability identifiers, trust scores, dependency relationships, and framework metadata. It can be fed into existing SBOM management tools and compliance dashboards.

CI/CD Integration and HTML Dashboard — How Does It Fit Into Development Workflows?

SkillFortify integrates into CI/CD pipelines as a CLI tool that returns structured JSON output. It also generates an HTML dashboard with visual summaries of scan results, dependency graphs, and trust score distributions. The dashboard is self-contained and requires no server infrastructure — it can be served from static storage or attached to CI/CD artifacts.

Benchmark Results — 96.95% F1 with Zero False Positives

SkillFortify’s benchmark results are the strongest in the agent security scanning space. On the 540-skill SkillFortifyBench dataset, the tool achieves:

Metric Value 95% Confidence Interval
F1 Score 96.95% [95.1%, 98.4%]
Precision 100% —
Recall 94.1% —
False Positive Rate 0% —
Average Scan Time 2.55 ms/skill —

The 100% precision and 0% false positive rate are the standout numbers. In enterprise security operations, false positives are the primary source of alert fatigue — security teams learn to ignore tools that cry wolf. SkillFortify’s formal approach means every alert is a real vulnerability, and every clean scan is a genuine clean bill of health.

The 94.1% recall means the tool misses approximately 5.9% of vulnerabilities. This is bounded by the DY-Skill model — vulnerabilities outside the model’s scope are not detected. However, the model is proven maximal for the five-phase skill lifecycle, so the recall gap represents attack vectors that fall outside the modeled threat landscape.

SkillFortifyBench — The 540-Skill Evaluation Framework

SkillFortifyBench is the evaluation dataset used to measure SkillFortify’s performance. It contains 540 skills across three formats (MCP, Claude Code, and OpenClaw), split evenly between 270 malicious skills (covering 13 attack types) and 270 benign skills (covering 5 categories).

The 13 attack types in the malicious set include prompt injection, tool poisoning, dependency confusion, credential theft, command injection, data exfiltration, privilege escalation, backdoor installation, supply chain substitution, manifest tampering, update hijacking, logic bomb, and time-of-check-time-of-use (TOCTOU) attacks.

The 5 benign categories cover utility tools, data processing, API wrappers, monitoring, and development helpers. This balanced design ensures the benchmark tests both detection capability and false positive resistance.

Comparison with Competitors

Heuristic Scanners — How Does SkillFortify Compare to SkillScan, skill-security-reviewer, and OWASP Agentic Scanner?

Analysis method Sound static analysis Heuristic + LLM + Docker LLM-based review Static analysis (heuristic)
Formal guarantees Yes No No No
Frameworks supported 22 ~3 ~2 ~5
False positive rate 0% Unknown Unknown Unknown

Offline capable Yes Partial No (LLM API) Yes
ASBOM generation Yes No No No
Trust scoring Formal algebra None None None
Dependency graph SAT-based ADG None None None
License Elastic 2.0 MIT MIT Apache 2.0

SkillScan (4 stars) combines static analysis with LLM behavioral prediction and Docker sandbox execution, but relies on heuristic methods with no formal guarantees. skill-security-reviewer (8 stars) uses LLM-based review — essentially asking an LLM to evaluate skill security, which inherits all the limitations of LLM reliability. OWASP Agentic Scanner (1 star) is the newest entrant, applying static analysis to OWASP Top 10 Agentic AI risks but still using heuristic pattern matching.

Why Formal Verification Matters More Than Pattern Matching

The fundamental difference is mathematical. Heuristic scanners can only detect vulnerabilities they have seen before and encoded as patterns. A novel attack — one that doesn’t match any existing rule — passes through undetected. Formal verification, by contrast, models the entire attack surface and can detect any attack that falls within the model’s scope, regardless of whether it has been seen before.

This is not a theoretical distinction. The ClawHavoc campaign used novel techniques that evaded all 12 heuristic scanners available at the time. A formal verification tool like SkillFortify, with its DY-Skill model covering the full skill lifecycle, would have detected those attacks because they fell within the modeled threat landscape.

Pricing and Licensing — Elastic License 2.0

SkillFortify is distributed under the Elastic License 2.0 (ELv2). This is a source-available license that permits use, modification, and distribution for non-production and internal business use, but restricts:

  • Providing the software as a managed service to third parties
  • Circumventing license key functionality
  • Removing or altering license notices

The ELv2 is not OSI-approved as an open source license, which has implications for enterprise procurement. Some organizations require OSI-approved licenses for their software supply chain. However, for internal security tooling, the ELv2 is generally acceptable — the restrictions primarily target cloud service providers who might offer SkillFortify as a hosted service.

The tool is free to use. There is no paid tier or enterprise license announced as of July 2026. The Qualixar platform may introduce commercial licensing in the future, but current access is unrestricted for all use cases permitted by the ELv2.

Real-World Use Cases

Enterprise Governance for Claude Code and Cursor Deployments

Organizations deploying Claude Code or Cursor across development teams need to ensure that agent skills don’t introduce supply chain vulnerabilities. SkillFortify can be integrated into the onboarding pipeline: every skill added to the team’s shared repository is scanned before it becomes available. The trust score and ASBOM provide auditable evidence for security reviews.

CI/CD Pipeline Security for Agentic Development

In CI/CD pipelines, agent skills can execute with significant privileges — reading secrets, modifying code, and deploying artifacts. SkillFortify scans skills at build time, failing the pipeline if a skill fails the security check. The lockfile ensures that the exact same skill versions are used in production as were scanned in CI.

Air-Gapped Environments and Offline-First Architecture

For defense, government, and financial sector deployments, air-gapped environments are common. SkillFortify’s offline-first architecture — no external API calls, no telemetry, no cloud dependency — makes it suitable for these environments. The tool can be installed via a single PyPI package and run entirely on isolated infrastructure.

Limitations and Considerations

Early Stage — 26 GitHub Stars, Single Author

SkillFortify has 26 GitHub stars and 5 open issues as of July 2026. The project is effectively a single-author tool. While the academic rigor is impressive, the community and ecosystem around the tool are minimal. Enterprise buyers should evaluate the bus factor and long-term maintenance prospects.

Elastic License vs Open Source

The Elastic License 2.0 is source-available but not OSI-approved open source. Organizations with strict open source policies may need legal review before adoption. The license also creates uncertainty about future pricing — if Qualixar introduces a paid tier, users of the free version may face feature limitations.

Python 3.11+ Requirement

SkillFortify requires Python 3.11 or later. Organizations still running Python 3.9 or 3.10 — which are still common in enterprise environments — will need to upgrade before adoption. This may be a non-trivial migration for teams with legacy infrastructure.

No Real-World Enterprise Case Studies Yet

The benchmark results are strong, but they are based on a synthetic benchmark (SkillFortifyBench) created by the same author. Independent third-party validation and real-world enterprise case studies are not yet available. The 0% false positive rate, while mathematically grounded, has not been validated in diverse production environments.

The Qualixar Ecosystem — Part of a Broader Reliability Platform

SkillFortify is one of 7 products in the Qualixar platform, which collectively address agent reliability across the full lifecycle. The Qualixar portfolio includes tools for agent testing, monitoring, observability, compliance, and security — all backed by peer-reviewed research. This ecosystem positioning is important: SkillFortify is not a standalone scanner but a component of a broader reliability infrastructure for AI agents.

The Qualixar platform has produced 7 peer-reviewed papers covering agent reliability topics. This academic foundation differentiates Qualixar from the typical open source security tool that relies on community contributions and ad-hoc methodology.

Conclusion — Is SkillFortify Ready for Enterprise?

SkillFortify represents a genuine breakthrough in AI agent security. It is the first tool to apply formal verification — sound static analysis with mathematical guarantees — to the problem of agent skill security. The benchmark results (96.95% F1, 100% precision, 0% false positive rate) are the strongest in the space, and the DY-Skill attacker model provides a formally grounded threat model that heuristic scanners cannot match.

For organizations already deploying AI agent frameworks at scale — particularly Claude Code, Cursor, MCP, or AutoGen — SkillFortify is worth evaluating today. The offline-first architecture, ASBOM generation, and CI/CD integration make it practical for real-world deployment. The zero false positive rate alone justifies the evaluation: if it performs as advertised, it eliminates the single biggest operational pain point in security scanning.

However, the tool is early stage. A single author, 26 GitHub stars, no independent validation, and an Elastic License 2.0 that may raise procurement concerns are real considerations. Enterprise buyers should run their own evaluation on their own skill repositories before committing.

The bottom line: SkillFortify is the most technically sophisticated agent security scanner available, and its formal verification approach is the right direction for the industry. It is not yet a mature enterprise product, but it is the tool that every organization using AI agents should be watching — and probably testing.
